item.title: DeepChopper: A Genomic Language Model that Cleans Up Nanopore Direct RNA Sequencing
item.description:
The chimera mystery
#

Direct RNA sequencing (dRNA-seq) on Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) platforms looks, on paper, like a transcriptomics dream. You sequence native RNA molecules end to end, you keep the modifications, and you skip every reverse-transcription and PCR step that has been quietly polluting short-read data for years. For a while, that was the story we were telling ourselves.

item.title: ChimeraLM: Structural Variant Detection in WGA Long-Read Sequencing
item.description: ChimeraLM is a language model for accurate structural variant detection in whole-genome amplified (WGA) long-read sequencing data. It is described in the paper A Language Model Enables Accurate Structural Variant Detection in Whole-Genome Amplified Long-Read Sequencing.

item.title: DeepChopper: Removing Chimeras in Nanopore Direct RNA Sequencing
item.description: DeepChopper is a genomic language model built on HyenaDNA that identifies and removes adapter-bridged chimera artifacts in nanopore direct RNA sequencing data. It is described in the paper Genomic Language Model Mitigates Chimera Artifacts in Nanopore Direct RNA Sequencing.

item.title: Interactive Visualization of Non-Linear Graphs with Aurora
PxBLAT: An Efficient and Ergonomic Python Binding Library for BLAT
Efficient Genomic Interval Search With a SIMD-Enhanced COITree
item.description:
Background
#

Bioinformatics researchers routinely work with many kinds of genomic data: DNA sequencing, RNA sequencing, and epigenetic assays among them. Much of that work comes down to manipulating genomic intervals, which is central to understanding the genetic basis of disease and to identifying therapeutic targets. A genomic interval is a region spanning a start and an end position; it can represent a gene, a regulatory element, or any other functional element of the genome. One primary application is the analysis of ChIP-seq data, where interval operations let us integrate ChIP-seq peaks with other data types such as gene expression and genetic variation. This integration gives a more complete picture of biological processes and of how they contribute to normal development or disease. Integrating these data types into a single data structure is challenging, however, especially for large datasets.

item.title: How to Use the Noodles Library in Rust
item.description:
Introduction
#

Noodles and rust-htslib are the two most widely used Rust libraries for working with genomic data. Both target the same file formats, but they take different approaches. This post walks through noodles, compares it with rust-htslib, and collects the pitfalls I ran into along the way.

item.title: BINARY: A Bioinformatics Algorithm Library in Modern C++
item.description: BINARY is a collection of algorithms and data structures built for modern C++ bioinformatics applications. You can use it directly in your own projects or as a component of a larger system. Every data structure and algorithm is implemented in modern C++ with an emphasis on efficiency.

item.title: BOSS: A Bioinformatics Toolbox in Modern C++
item.description: BOSS is a bioinformatics toolbox written in modern C++. Each tool is designed to be easy to use and fast, and the whole codebase is tested exhaustively. BOSS is free software distributed under the GNU General Public License v3.

item.title: Building a C++ Development Environment With htslib
item.description:
Configure the compile environment
#

I am planning to develop a tool in C++ that runs on both Linux and macOS. The recurring obstacle is that I usually lack root access, so I cannot simply run apt-get install for dependencies on Ubuntu. Working through the dependency chain and compiling each library by hand takes anywhere from a night to a week.

item.title: Building Phylogenetic Trees with Neighbor Joining in Python
item.description: Neighbor joining (NJ) is a distance-based method for building phylogenetic trees. Given a matrix of pairwise distances between taxa, it repeatedly merges the closest pair of clusters until it has produced an unrooted tree with edge lengths. This post walks through the algorithm and then presents my full Python implementation, which also computes bootstrap support values for the resulting tree.
